role: The second reading: each entry read to refute it, not to admire it.
method: Each fragment read whole beside what show.cjs prints for the grape (GRAPES_PLUS and GRAPES, TASTE, INTRO_GRAPES, GRID_SAY, GRID_READS, the service rows) and beside the Codex region records for Burgundy, Beaujolais, Oregon, Washington, New York, British Columbia, Austria and Burgenland, Sopron, Eger and Hungary, Württemberg, South Africa, Stellenbosch, Walker Bay, Paarl and the Swartland, Chile and Itata, Provence and Lebanon.

Every fact the reviewed records do not already state was put to search: the skin of Cinsault, its planting in Chile and Secano Interior; the Neusiedlersee rule and its year, Rotburger and the campaign of 2018; the Bikavér rules and the soils of the Burgenland origins; the cause of the paint note in Pinotage and its respelling; the Bourgogne label and the name of Pinot Noir; Gamay Beaujolais in American law.

The glass read as a blind taster: each note asked whether a taster would nod, each prose field scanned by the lint for a family word in disguise, each ladder set beside the Codex climate line for the place, and each tell checked from both sides so that no tell parts two grapes by a note both carry.

Each Old World and New World entry (Pinot Noir, Gamay and Cinsault) read for a false or lazy generalisation, the exceptions in blur and a call that would survive a flight; each home and abroad pair (Zweigelt, Blaufränkisch and Pinotage) read for the same and against TASTE.world.

The four lines counted and said aloud for the five beats in order; the sale read for its two sentences and for whether it is said to the guest, and for a hook another grape already uses; the cards and questions read for one key, four options of one kind and a stem that gives nothing away.

node .scripts/grapes/build-grapes.cjs --lint --chunk g8 run after every round of edits until it printed six of six sound. The writing build was never run and no file but the six fragments and this record was touched.
limits: This session reached search alone; no source page was opened, so a page is cited as the search results quoted it, and every address the authors gave stays unopened.
The brief allows five searches a grape. Pinot Noir took two, Gamay two, Zweigelt two, Blaufränkisch two, Pinotage two and Cinsault four.
A source whose address or title names a person is left out (several writers sites came back for Itata, Bikavér and Pinotage), and the fact is cited from another page or from the Codex record.
The Syrah, Cabernet Franc, Zinfandel and Grenache entries do not compare Blaufränkisch, Pinotage or Cinsault, so those tells were read from one side only.

pinot-noir.verdict: Sound after three fixes. The respelling, the German, Italian and Austrian names, the Oregon floor, the climate rungs and the service figures hold; the two cellar lines set a Burgundy habit on the New World side, and one label line said less than the law allows.
tested: say against GRID_SAY (PEE-noh NWAHR): opens on it, with Spätburgunder after a comma; the Codex Ahr, Baden and Pfalz records say the German name the same way, give or take the break.
The names abroad: Spätburgunder in Germany, Pinot Nero in Italy, Blauburgunder in Austria and the Alto Adige. Agree with the Codex and the sources.
The Oregon floor of 90 per cent against the federal 75: the Codex Washington and Oregon records state it.
The ladder against the Court grid: the Côte d Or and the Willamette Valley cool, Carneros, Sonoma and the Central Coast moderate. Agrees; no warm rung, rightly.
Structure against the reviewed profile (body light to medium, acid medium plus to high, tannin low to medium and silky, alcohol moderate to medium plus): agrees.
The cellar lines against the Codex Burgundy record: the cold soak, set as a New World mark, is Burgundy own habit; whole bunches are a choice there, not a habit.
The label line Bourgogne Rouge: the sources read disagree on whether the front label may carry the grape, and many regional labels print Pinot Noir; seldom names the grape could not stand.

The glass as a blind taster: every note is in the reviewed profile or the grid reads (red cherry, raspberry, strawberry, cranberry, black cherry, plum, rose, violet, mushroom, forest floor, beetroot, cola, baking spice named as clove and cinnamon).

Service against the reference rows: 12 to 15 degrees Celsius, the Burgundy bowl, decanting usually unnecessary and a fragile old bottle poured gently. Agrees. Age against TASTE (five to twenty): agrees.
The four lines counted (23, 40, 105 and 40 words) and said aloud: the five beats in order, the pine cone hedged as said to come.
Compare tells from both sides: Grenache and Meunier name Pinot Noir and agree; the Gamay tell agrees once forest floor leaves the Gamay notes.
Cards and questions: the worlds question keyed on moderate California with three cooler, tarter Old World options; one key each, nothing given away.

changed.why: Seldom names the grape is contested: regional Bourgogne may carry the grape and many labels do, and the sources read disagree only on the front label. The new line stands on the Codex Beaujolais record.

gamay.verdict: Sound after eight fixes. The edict of 1395, the ten crus in order, Nouveau, the Gamay Beaujolais rule of 2007 and the service figures hold; the New World side made Oregon and Ontario Gamay a Pinot Noir in all but name, against the Codex Oregon record, and forest floor stood among the notes though both entries and the reviewed profile part Pinot Noir from Gamay by it.
tested: say against GRID_SAY (gah-MAY): the same.

The edict of 1395, the ten crus in order north to south, Nouveau on the third Thursday of November, Beaujolais in law a part of greater Burgundy, semi carbonic the norm and the crus increasingly made like Burgundy: all in the Codex Beaujolais record.
Gamay Beaujolais: barred from American labels of wine bottled on or after 9 April 2007 by the federal rule, and the vine a clone of Pinot Noir. Confirmed.
The New World side against the Codex Oregon record, which calls Oregon Gamay bright and crunchy in the Beaujolais manner: the entry made it a Pinot Noir in all but name in five places.
The spoken line against the entry own New World glass: firmer against rounder.
The glass as a blind taster, and every tell from both sides: forest floor stood among the Gamay notes although both the Pinot Noir and the Gamay tells part the two by it.
Structure against the reviewed profile (body light, medium in the crus, acid high, tannin low, alcohol moderate): agrees. Age against TASTE (young, though cru Beaujolais keeps ten): agrees.
The four lines counted (22, 38, 105 and 39 words) and said aloud: five beats, the crus explained in the same breath.
Cards and questions: one key each; the label question options are four labels of one region, and the worlds question keys the typical style.

changed.was: Gamay was banished from the heart of Burgundy in 1395, and it found its home to the south, on the granite hills of Beaujolais. It is light and bright, with sour cherry, raspberry and violet, high acidity and hardly any tannin. Most of it ferments as whole bunches in a sealed vat, which keeps the fruit fresh and can add a hint of banana. Oregon and Ontario tend to make it as they make Pinot Noir, a little darker and firmer. zweigelt.verdict: Sound after six fixes. The crossing of 1922 at Klosterneuburg, Rotburger and Blauer Zweigelt on the label, the Neusiedlersee rule of at least 60 per cent and its year, and the abroad list hold; the respelling departed from the Codex records, one label line claimed more than the sources show, and the Okanagan is no cold place.
tested: The crossing of Blaufränkisch and Saint Laurent at Klosterneuburg in 1922: the Codex Austria record.
The respelling against the Codex records: TSVY-gelt in the Austria, Burgenland and Sopron records; the entry wrote TSVYE.
Neusiedlersee: created in 2012 in the Codex record, from the 2011 vintage in the press; the Reserve at least 60 per cent Zweigelt. The card year agrees with the Codex.

Rotburger and Blauer Zweigelt as legal names; the breeder a member of the National Socialist party; the campaign of 2018 to rename the grape. Confirmed. That a few growers prefer Rotburger: no source.
Abroad against the Codex: the Okanagan is hot in summer, so cold places could not stand.
The profile written new against the Régionale row (acidity, body and tannin all medium; sour cherry, pepper, juicy): agrees.
The four lines counted and said aloud; the sale spoke of a guest in the third person.
Compare tells from both sides: Blaufränkisch and Gamay name Zweigelt and agree; sour cherry is carried by both Zweigelt and Gamay and parted nothing.
Cards and questions: one key each; the blind question distractors are weak but wrong.

changed.was: Gamay is paler and lighter, with violet and often a candied banana note; Zweigelt is darker, with sour cherry, pepper and a touch more tannin.
changed.now: Gamay is paler and lighter, with violet and often a candied banana note; Zweigelt is darker, with a peppery snap and a touch more tannin.
changed.why: Gamay carries sour cherry too, so the tell parted nothing by it.

changed.was: TSVYE-gelt. The Z is said as ts and the W as v, in two syllables with the weight on the first.
changed.now: TSVY-gelt. The Z is said as ts and the W as v, in two syllables with the weight on the first.
changed.why: The respelling said in the answer follows say.

blaufrankisch.verdict: Sound after seven fixes. The three Burgenland origins and their soils, Mittelburgenland and the Eisenberg as Blaufränkisch alone, Rosalia, Kékfrankos as the backbone of Bikavér, Lemberger in Württemberg, Washington and the Finger Lakes all hold; the respelling departed from the Codex records, the cool rung set the Eisenberg among cool sites on no source, and the forty-five second line opened by making Burgenland the grape birthplace.
tested: The three origins against the Codex Burgenland record: Mittelburgenland and Eisenberg Blaufränkisch alone, Leithaberg at least 85 per cent, Rosalia Blaufränkisch or Zweigelt; the soils, deep clay, limestone and schist, iron rich slate. Agree, and two trade sources agree on the soils.
Bikavér: Kékfrankos at least 30 per cent in Eger and at least 45 in Szekszárd, with Kadarka at least 5 there; the Codex calls it the compulsory backbone. Agrees.
Sopron: the Codex Sopron record calls Kékfrankos cool, peppery and bright and Sopron its capital, and its Deutschkreutz record puts Sopron across the border from Mittelburgenland.
The ladder against the Codex: no record or source calls the Eisenberg cool; Sopron, Württemberg and the Finger Lakes are cool or marginal in the Codex records; Mittelburgenland a warm basin.
The respelling against the Codex records: BLAU-fren-kish, KAYK-frahn-kosh, LEM-bair-ger.
Lemberger in Washington and the Finger Lakes, and not Limburger the cheese: the Codex Washington and New York records.
Structure against the reviewed profile and the Régionale row: the entry follows the reviewed profile, as the author said.
The four lines counted (22, 38, 106 and 43 words) and said aloud: the opening made Burgenland the grape birthplace.
Compare tells from both sides: Zweigelt names Blaufränkisch and agrees; Syrah and Cabernet Franc read from this side only.

changed.now: Kékfrankos in Hungary, where Sopron is called its capital and it is the backbone of Egri Bikavér. Lemberger in Germany, grown chiefly in Württemberg.
changed.why: Sopron is called its capital, as the Codex Sopron record says; backbone for frames, as in the Kékfrankos label line.

changed.was: Blaufränkisch comes from Burgenland, the eastern edge of Austria along the Hungarian border, and it is the country's red with backbone. It tastes of black cherry and blackberry with a note of cracked black pepper, on bright acidity, firm tannin and a medium to full body. The lighter wines are raised in steel or large old casks and the fuller ones in oak barrels, with less new wood than a generation ago. Pour it with roast duck, venison or a goulash rich with paprika. Hungary calls the same grape Kékfrankos and Germany calls it Lemberger, so you may have met it under another name.
changed.now: Blaufränkisch is at home in Burgenland, the eastern edge of Austria along the Hungarian border, and it is the country's red with backbone. It tastes of black cherry and blackberry with a note of cracked black pepper, on bright acidity, firm tannin and a medium to full body. The lighter wines are raised in steel or large old casks and the fuller ones in oak barrels, with less new wood than a generation ago. Pour it with roast duck, venison or a goulash rich with paprika. Hungary calls the same grape Kékfrankos and Germany calls it Lemberger, so you may have met it under another name.
changed.why: Comes from reads as the grape birthplace, which is not settled in Burgenland: the author own report gives a parentage that points to the wider Danube lands.

pinotage.verdict: Sound after four fixes. The crossing at Stellenbosch in 1925, Hermitage, the label of 1961, the Cape Blend at 30 to 70 per cent with no law behind it, the Wine of Origin scheme of 1973 and the cause of the paint and banana note hold; the respelling departed from the Codex records, the sale and the spoken line claimed the grape grew nowhere else, and the ladder set the Codex own cool sites on the moderate rung and a cool corner on the warm one.
tested: The crossing at Stellenbosch in 1925 of Pinot Noir and Cinsaut, then called Hermitage: the Codex South Africa record.
The Wine of Origin scheme of 1973, and Stellenbosch, Paarl and Swartland as districts: the Codex record.
The paint and banana note: the Codex record and the research read both put it down to fermenting hot and fast, the research adding stressed vines and the yeast. The guest answer stands.
The respelling against the Codex records (PEE-no-tahzh, PEE-noh-tahzh) and three pronunciation guides, none of which gives PIN.
The ladder against the Codex climate lines: Walker Bay cool maritime and its Pinotage cool climate; the Simonsberg a cooler corner; Swartland Pinotage lighter and whole bunch.
The spoken line and the sale against the entry own abroad line: the grape is grown a little elsewhere.
Structure against the reviewed profile: agrees, as the author said.
Compare tells: Syrah and Zinfandel from this side only; Cinsault does not compare Pinotage.
Cards and questions: one key each; Abraham Perold, long dead, named where the card asks who crossed it.

changed.was: Pinotage could only be South African: it was bred at Stellenbosch in 1925, and few other countries grow it at all. It makes a dark, full red that tastes of black plum, mulberry and wood smoke, with firm tannin and a warm finish. The classic style is aged in oak barrels and built to keep, and a popular modern one uses heavily toasted oak to give a clear taste of coffee and chocolate. It belongs beside a fire: pour it with grilled lamb, barbecued ribs or smoked sausage. Ask where the name comes from and you have its parents: Pinot Noir, and Cinsault, which the Cape used to call Hermitage.

cinsault.verdict: Sound after five fixes. Hermitage, Cinsaut, Ottavianello, the planting in Chile after the Chillán earthquake of 1939, Secano Interior for País and Cinsault and the Bekaa hold; the guest answer and one explanation gave the grape thin skins where the sources give it fairly thick, firm ones, and the worlds question admitted a second key.
tested: The skin: an encyclopedia and the United States germplasm record give large berries with fairly thick or firm skins; the entry said thin, twice.
Chile: planted in the southern hills after the Chillán earthquake of 1939 in several sources and the Codex Chile record, officially 1940 in one.
Secano Interior reserved for País and Cinsault: the Codex Chile record, citing the decree; not confirmed or refuted by the pages read.
Cinsaut as the French official and Cape spelling, Hermitage at the Cape, Ottavianello in Puglia: confirmed.
The Bekaa as an old Cinsault home: the Codex Lebanon record.
Côtes de Provence against the Codex Provence record: an appellation, the largest, with Cinsault the rosé grape above all.
The profile written new against the Régionale row (warm to hot, acid medium, light body and tannin, a blender often for rosé, a parent of Pinotage): agrees.
The worlds question: the blur line admits the Languedoc bottling Cinsault alone and the Cape blending it, so a second pair could be defended until the stem asked for the typical pair.
The four lines counted (20, 39, 106 and 36 words) and said aloud.

changed.was: Nothing at all. Cinsault has big berries and thin skins, so there is little colour or tannin to draw out. The pale colour is the grape, and the flavour is all there.
changed.now: Nothing at all. Cinsault has large, juicy berries, so there is more juice to each skin and less colour and tannin to draw out. The pale colour is the grape.
changed.why: The sources read give Cinsault large berries with fairly thick, firm skins, not thin ones; its pale colour comes from the share of juice to skin.

codexRecords: The Eger record (js/regions/hungary.json, eger) says Egri Bikavér is made from at least three varieties; the sources read for this check say four, with Kékfrankos at 30 per cent or more. The table gives no count. The owner may want the record checked against the Eger product specification.

The Régionale row for Zweigelt (INTRO_GRAPES) calls it Austria most planted red, and the Codex Austria and Burgenland records say the same of Austria and of Burgenland: a fact the house rules count volatile. The table says the everyday red.

The Codex respells Blaufränkisch BLAU-fren-kish in the Austria and Burgenland records and BLAU-frenk-ish in the New York record, and Kékfrankos KAYK-frahn-kosh in most records and KAYK-fron-kosh in the Szekszárd one: the same sounds, the break or the vowel moved. The table follows the Austria and Hungary records.
The Codex respells Pinotage PEE-no-tahzh in the South Africa record and PEE-noh-tahzh in the Walker Bay record: the same sounds. The table follows the second, which matches the house form of Pinot.
The Neusiedlersee DAC is dated created in 2012 in the Codex Burgenland record and from the 2011 vintage in the press; both can stand, and the Zweigelt card follows the Codex.

Secano Interior as a term reserved for País and Cinsault stands on the Codex Chile record; the trade pages read for this check treat the Secano Interior as a wider area of patrimonial grapes and do not mention the reserve. Not shown wrong.
unsettled: Whether every source address still answers: none could be opened from this session.
Whether a regional Bourgogne may print the grape on its front label: the sources read disagree. The table no longer says either way.

How much Oregon and Ontario Gamay is made whole bunch and how much destemmed: the Codex Oregon record says the Beaujolais manner, one trade source says mostly as Pinot Noir is. The table hedges both ways.
Whether the breeder of Zweigelt named the grape Rotburger, and the year it took his name (1975 in most sources, 1978 in one): the table says neither.
The year Chile planted Cinsault in the south: 1939 in most sources, officially 1940 in one. The table says just after the earthquake of 1939.
The Egri Bikavér count of varieties, three in the Codex and four in the sources: the table gives none.
settled: Gamay Beaujolais may not appear on labels of American wine bottled on or after 9 April 2007, and the vine was a clone of Pinot Noir.
Cinsault has large berries with fairly thick, firm skins and resists drought; it is sold as a table grape as well.
Neusiedlersee DAC Reserve may be pure Zweigelt or a blend of at least 60 per cent Zweigelt with other local reds.
Austrian law admits Zweigelt, Blauer Zweigelt and Rotburger on the label; the breeder was a member of the National Socialist party, and a campaign of 2018 asked for the name to change.
Kékfrankos is the leading grape of both Bikavér blends: at least 30 per cent in Eger, at least 45 in Szekszárd with at least 5 of Kadarka.
The Leithaberg lies on limestone and schist, the Eisenberg on iron rich soils over slate, Mittelburgenland on heavy loam and clay.
Isoamyl acetate, the banana and paint note of rushed Pinotage, forms when the fermentation runs too hot, and stressed vines and the yeast add to it.
The cold soak and the choice over whole bunches are Burgundy own habits, so neither marks the New World.
